title: Number of 1 Bits
description:
Given a non-negative integer `n` representing an unsigned 32-bit value, return the number of bits that are set to `1` in its binary representation. This quantity is also called the Hamming weight or population count.

Do not rely on a built-in popcount; manipulate the bits yourself.
hints: Check the lowest bit with n & 1, then shift right. Repeat up to 32 times.
Faster: n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit. Count how many times you can do that before reaching zero. This loops once per set bit instead of once per bit.
approach:
**Key insight: `n & (n - 1)` removes exactly the lowest set bit of `n`. Repeating until `n` is zero therefore takes exactly as many iterations as there are set bits.**

Why the identity holds: subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit to 0 and every bit below it to 1; AND-ing with the original keeps all higher bits, zeroes the lowest set bit, and the bits below it were already 0.

**Simpler version:** loop 32 times, add `n & 1`, shift right. Always 32 iterations; fine, but the Brian Kernighan trick above is what interviewers expect you to know.

**Branch-free version (worth mentioning):** the SWAR popcount adds bit pairs, then nibbles, then bytes with masks `0x55555555`, `0x33333333`, `0x0F0F0F0F` and a final multiply; it is what `__builtin_popcount` compiles to without hardware support. Python's `int.bit_count()` does this natively.

**Common mistakes:** in Java or C, treating the input as signed and using `>>` (arithmetic shift) on a negative value, which loops forever; use `>>>` or compare against 0 after the shift. Python has unbounded ints, so no issue, but say you know.

**Interview follow-ups:** (1) Counting Bits: popcount of every number from 0 to `n` in `O(n)` total. (2) Hamming Distance between two numbers is popcount of their XOR. (3) Check whether `n` is a power of two: `n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0`.

complexity.time: O(k) where k is the number of set bits, at most 32
